  • Generated by tools/ebl_fetch.py on 2026-10-16 – do not edit by hand; re-run the tool instead.

Per line: N = normalized Akkadian reconstruction (| metrical foot, || caesura); T = eBL English translation; L = lemmas with eBL dictionary glosses; then notes, parallel lines, and the manuscripts' transliterations (ATF). Bibliography keys like [RN117: 889] are resolved in bibliography.md (RN117 = George 2003).

1

  • N: inūma | ilū | awīlum
  • T: When gods were man,
  • L: inūma ← inūma I “when Bab.”; ilū ← ilu I “pl. ilū, ilānu god, deity a or the god, also du.”; awīlum ← awīlu I “man human being (also coll.)”
  • Note: The interpretation of the first line of Atramḫasīs gave rise to a famous controversy between the two most prominent Assyriologists of the second half of the 20th century, W. G. Lambert and W. von Soden. The former interpreted the ending -um in awīlum as a locative-adverbial case with comparative value, “When the gods like men bore the work” ([RN435: 146]). The second claimed that the locative-adverbial with comparative value is unknown in Akkadian, and therefore the two lines must be taken independently, the first one as a nominal sentence: “Als die Götter (auch noch) Mensch waren, trugen sie die Mühsal” ([RN7444: 416–417], [soden1978erste: 76]; see also [RN235: 127 with fn. 2]) — an interpretation rejected by Lambert as theologically impossible, since in Mesopotamian mythology the gods are never portrayed as having once been men. The discovery of the incipit of the Neo-Assyrian version (enūma ilū kī amēli, by [RN2709: 534–535]) seemed to confirm Lambert’s interpretation, but von Soden’s solution, which he justified in detail in [RN7456: 312–313], has been followed by many interpreters (cf. the title of Bottéro’s monograph, Lorsque les dieux faisaient l’homme). See in general [matous1967neuern: 5 fn. 29], [RN630: 23–25], and [ziegler2016aqba] for a summary of older and more recent discussions on this line. Interpreters in subsequent years have mostly aligned with one or the other solution. In Lambert’s camp, [loesov2004inuma: 197-98] interpreted the case marker -um in awīlum as a locative with functional (not comparative) meaning and offered the translation: “When gods –in place of man–” (similarly already [oberhuber1982versuch: 279–281]). On the basis of a passage in the Old Babylonian letter A.1246, [ziegler2016aqba: 115–17] shows that the comparative locative is already attested in literary Old Babylonian and could therefore also be used in this line. Supporting von Soden’s interpretation, [moran1971atrahasis: 59 fn. 2] chose to translate “When (some) gods were mankind”; [groneberg1978terminativ: 20] stated the form awīlum should be interpreted as nominative singular with an intended comparison (“als die Götter wie Menschen waren”); and [seux1981notes] supported Groneberg’s interpretation by pointing out the passages I 93 bēlī bīnu būnūka and I 95 ellil bīnu būnūka (q.v., following [RN1445: 158]), where the same construction can be found ([RN600: 38] rejected this interpretation of Groneberg and Seux). In Jacobsen’s idiosyncratic interpretation ([jacobsen1977inuma: 114–115]: “When Ilu was the boss”), ilu is a singular that refers to the god Enlil and awīlum denotes a person of authority. [Kilmer1996: 134] (see also [kilmer2000: 97]) associates awīlum with the Semitic root for labor (*ʿw/ml); similarly, [RN344: 308 with fn. 32] interprets awīlum here as a metonymy for “slave.” A different interpretation, which seems to bring a synthesis to both lines of thought, is that of [LS25: 652], who interprets awīlum as a predicative complement, and therefore simply a nominative: “When gods, being human, carried out the labour…” This is the interpretation followed here. Note that the variant with the preposition kī(ma) is now attested in an Old Babylonian tablet (i-nu-ma i-lu ki-ma a-wi-li in [RN2979: 162 No. 55 l. 15]). For the metric analysis of the passage in lines I 1-6 see further [RN3041: 182–83]; for the relationship between the beginning of Atramḫasīs and Enki and Ninmaḫ see [RN838: 18–37].
SipOB1 i 1. i#-nu-ma i-lu# a#-wi#-lum

2

  • N: ublū | dulla(m) || izbilū | šupš[i]kka(m)
  • T: They did forced labor, they bore drudgery.
  • L: ublū ← wabālu I “(cf. also babālu) to carry, bring”; dulla(m) ← dullu I “pl. m. & f. trouble”; izbilū ← zabālu I “to carry, deliver”; šupš[i]kka(m) ← tupšikku I “pl. f. brick-carrying frame”
SipOB1 i 2. ub-lu du-ul-la# iz-bi-lu šu#-up-š[i-i]k-ka

3

  • N: šupšik (|) ilī | rabī-ma
  • T: Great indeed was the drudgery of the gods,
  • L: šupšik ← tupšikku I “pl. f. brick-carrying frame”; ilī ← ilu I “pl. ilū, ilānu god, deity a or the god, also du.”; rabī-ma ← rabû II “to be big, to grow”
  • Note: As noted by [jacobsen1977inuma: 117 fn. 24] there is a pun between šupšik and šapšāqum.
SipOB1 i 3. šu-up#-ši-ik i-li ra-bi-[m]a

4

  • N: dullum | kabit || mād | šapšāqum
  • T: The forced labor was heavy, the misery too much:
  • L: dullum ← dullu I “pl. m. & f. trouble”; kabit ← kabātu I “to be(come) heavy”; mād ← mâdu I “to be(come) many, numerous”; šapšāqum ← šapšāqu I “constraint, hardship Bab.(lit.) of human condition(s)”
  • Note: See the analysis of the stylistic features of Atramḫasīs I 1–6 in [RN344: 509-510].
SipOB1 i 4. du-ul-lu-um# ka-bi-it ma-a-ad ša-ap-ša#-qum

5

  • N: rabûtum | anunnakū | sebettam
  • T: The great Anunna-gods, the seven, were burdening
  • L: rabûtum ← rabû I “big”; anunnakū ← Anunnakkū I “(the) gods”; sebettam ← sebettu I “group of seven, heptad”
  • Note: The interpretation of the line has been the subject of much discussion. On the one hand, the accusative case of the number “seven” is unusual: for this reason, [RN7444: 420–421] (and already [soden1966igigu: 142]) interpreted the line as enjambement and thus connected “seven” with Igigu in the next line, which appears in the accusative case. Other interpretations are, however, possible: [lambert1980line: 84-85] interprets it as accusative of relation. Similarly, [RN1445: 157] compares the line with Etana @url{/corpus/L/1/9/OB/Morgan#10}{OB Morgan 10} (sebetta bābū) and Anzû @url{/corpus/L/1/10/OB/II#38}{OB II 38//40} (sebettam qablī, cp. @url{/corpus/L/1/10/SB/II#30}{SB II 30//150} sebet qablī). [RN2009: 161] and [RN1196: 75] interprets it as an adverbial phrase. A radically different interpretation is offered by [RN344: 509–510 with note 713 and 715], according to whom “seven” means “seven times” (referring to dullum), so “sevenfold (work).” Metzler also discusses other possible interpretations.
SipOB1 i 5. ra#-bu-tum {d}a-nun#-na-ku se-be₂-et-tam

6

  • N: dullam | ušazbalū | ig[īg]ī
  • T: The Igigi-gods with forced labor.
  • L: dullam ← dullu I “pl. m. & f. trouble”; ušazbalū ← zabālu I “to carry, deliver”; ig[īg]ī ← Igigû I “the (ten) great gods O/jB”
SipOB1 i 6. du#-ul-lam u₂-ša-az-ba-lu# {d}i-g[i-g]i

7

  • N: ānu | abūšunu | ša[rr]u
  • T: Anu their father was king,
  • L: ānu ← Anu I “An(um) (the god of heaven) OAkk, Bab.”; abūšunu ← abu I “father (st. constr. abi, occas. abu, ab”; ša[rr]u ← šarru I “pl. šarrū, šarrānu king”
SipOB1 i 7. a#-nu a-bu-šu#-nu ša[r-r]u

8

  • N: [m]ālikšunu | qurād[u] | ellil
  • T: Their counsellor was the warrior Enlil,
  • L: [m]ālikšunu ← māliku I “adviser, counsellor”; qurād[u] ← qurādu I “hero, warrior of god, king, soldiers”; ellil ← Ellil I “”
SipOB1 i 8. [m]a-li-ik#-šu#-nu# qu₂-ra-d[u] {d#}+en-lil₂

9

  • N: [ku]zzalûšun[u] | [ni]nurta
  • T: Their prefect was Ninurta,
  • L: [ku]zzalûšun[u] ← guzalû I “OB pl. f. chair-carrier, throne-bearer O/jB OB (an official)”; [ni]nurta ← Ninurta I
SipOB1 i 9. [ku-u]z-za-lu#-šu#-n[u] {d}[ni]n-urta

10

  • N: [u] gallûšunu | [enn]ūgi
  • T: [And] their bailiff(?) [En]nugi.
  • L: [u] ← u I “and, but, also”; gallûšunu ← gallû I “(a demon) Bab. also transf., as desig. of enemy”; [enn]ūgi ← Ennugi I
SipOB1 i 10. [u₃] gal-lu-šu-nu {d#}+[en-n]u-gi

11

  • N: mātam | īhuzū | lētīša
  • T: They had occupied the borders of the earth,
  • L: mātam ← mātu I “f. land, country”; īhuzū ← ahāzu I “to take”; lētīša ← lētu I “f. cheek”
  • Note: [RN435: 42-43] read the line as qātam īhuzū qātīša and translated “The gods had clasped hands together.” von Soden read the first sign as [k]u- (cf. kūtum “jug”), and interpreted qātum as the handle of a vessel: “Sie fassten die (Los-)Flasche an ihrem Henkel” (see [RN7444: 421-422]). According to von Soden, this line describes part of the process of decision by casting lots described in the next line. After collation of the tablet (a collation confirmed by A. Shaffer’s examination apud [RN7457: 100] and later by the first-millennium version), von Soden corrected his reading to [k]u!-tam i-hu-zu le-ti-ša “die (Los-)Flasche fassten sie an ihrer ‘Wange’ (= Flaschenhals?)” ([RN7456: 314]; see also [vonsoden1994atram: 618]). The reading of the first sign as ku- was considered unlikely by [RN1447: 97] (drawing in [RN1447: 98 A]) and [RN118: 184]; the latter consider šu- more likely. Collation of the passage in the Standard Babylonian version (q.v.) suggests the reading adopted here, which is also compatible with the traces. The “cheeks” of the land appear also in @url{/fragmentarium/IM.67692}{IM.67692} l. 15.
SipOB1 i 11. ma*#-tam i-hu-zu le#-ti-ša

12

  • N: isqam | iddû || ilū | izzūzū
  • T: They cast lots, the gods took their shares:
  • L: isqam ← isqu I “pl. usu. f. lot”; iddû ← nadû III “to throw (down)”; ilū ← ilu I “pl. ilū, ilānu god, deity a or the god, also du.”; izzūzū ← zâzu I “to divide”
SipOB1 i 12. is-qa₂-am id-du-u₂ i-lu# iz-zu#-zu

13

  • N: ānum | īteli | šamêša(m)
  • T: Anu went up to heaven,
  • L: ānum ← Anu I “An(um) (the god of heaven) OAkk, Bab.”; īteli ← elû III “to go up, arise”; šamêša(m) ← šamû I “mostly pl. tant. sky, heaven”
  • Note: On the ending -(i)ša(m), see [RN27201: 67g*], [RN435: 148], [pettinato1970review: 77], [RN1013: 43], and [RN2787: 192–193].
SipOB1 i 13. a#-nu# i-te-li ša#-me#-e#-ša

14

  • N: [ellil | ī]huz || erṣetam | baʾūlātuššu
  • T: [Enlil too]k the earth for his subjects,
  • L: [ellil ← Ellil I “”; ī]huz ← ahāzu I “to take”; erṣetam ← erṣetu I “earth, land”; baʾūlātuššu ← ba'ūlātu I “(jB cf. also bahūlātu) people, subjects OAkk, Bab.(lit.), of…”
  • Note: The recovery of the Standard Babylonian version has made von Soden’s reading of the line (e.g. [soden1978erste: 77]: er-ṣe-tam-ma pa-la-[t]u?-uš-šu; see [RN630: 29]). [RN435: 43] translated the last word as “… his subjects”, Wilcke ([RN2009: 160 with fn. 12–14]) “Herrschafts-, Verfügungsbereich,” since according to him baʾūlātu(m) represent the word beʾūlātu(m), “Verfügungs, Betriebskapital,” known from economic documents. The restoration of the beginning is given by [RN118: 184]: “The OB text is probably to be read [{den-lil i]-hu#-uz#} (coll.)” (see also the previous collation in [RN435: pl. 11]).
SipOB1 i 14. [{d}+en-lil₂ i]-hu*#-uz*# er#-ṣe#-tam ba-u₂-la-tu#-uš-šu

15

  • N: [šigar]a | nahbalu (|) tiāmtim
  • T: [The bolt], the trap of the sea,
  • L: [šigar]a ← šigaru I “(wooden) clamp (neck-)stock for captives”; nahbalu ← nahbalu I “trap O/jB pitfall for lions etc., box-trap”; tiāmtim ← tiāmtu I “jB pl. also timiāti sea”
SipOB1 i 15. [ši-ga-ra n]a-ah-ba-lu ti-a-am-tim

16

  • N: [itta]d[n]ū | ana enki | naššīki
  • T: [They had gi]ven to Enki the leader.
  • L: [itta]d[n]ū ← nadānu II “to give”; ana ← ana I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”; enki ← Enki I; naššīki ← niššīku I “(a title of Ea) O/jB”
  • Note: Collation of the first preserved signs in [RN435: pl. 11].
SipOB1 i 16. [it-ta-a]d?-[n]u* a+na {d#}+en#-ki na#-aš#-ši-ki#

17

  • Note: Several proposals as for the reading of the signs before itti ellil have been made. Thus, [pettinato1970review: 78] read qa-ab#-la#-am (but /qa/ is normally written qá). [RN7444: 424] suggested “wohl da!-ba!-ba-am it-ti {den-lil₂}, ‘mit Enlil zu reden’”; and added: “na-ba-ba-am (vgl. [RN2720: 694a] zu nabābu) wäre aber auch nicht ganz undenkbar, wenn die Spuren zu da- nicht passen sollten” (see also [soden1978erste: 62]: u[b-la] pi₂-i-ni na-ba-ba-am it-ti {den-lil₂}, “hat unser Mund [vorgebracht,] daß wir uns bei Enlil beklagen”). [RN2709: 537] rejected von Soden’s first proposal, but thought the second to be possible (“Not da!-ba-ba-am, though na-ba-ba-am can be considered”; see also his collation in [RN435: pl. 11]). [westhuizen1986some: 92] read na-ka#-ra#-am? (as already suggested by [aro1971atram: 176]), so the meaning would be ub-la pi-i-ni na-ka-ra-am it-ti {den-lil₂} “(Now, every single one of us gods) has spoken in favour of hostility against Enlil”, but this reading does not fit the traces (see [RN118: 186]: “The alternative reading proposed by J. P. van der Westhuizen (…) is not supported by the traces (coll.)”; and [RN164: 279]: “The proposal of Westhuizen (…) is excluded by collation”). If the reading of the signs as na#-ba?#-ba?#-am# is correct, one may consider parsing it as N infinitive of the naprās- form (on which see [RN27201: §56h]; [BB07kk: 175]) of the verb abābu, “ravage” vel sim. (on which see [jimenez2021zweite: 289]). The SB version has mithuṣa instead.

[tropper1987seele] and [tropper1989nekromantie: 49-56] interprets eṭemmum as the human component in the creation of mankind, contrasting it with the flesh (šīrum) and blood (dāmum) of the slaughtered god. He advocates for translating eṭemmum as “Totengeist” (“dead ghost”), which opposes “living human being” (balṭu) in the subsequent line. [groneberg1990unterwelt: 252-53] also supports the translation “Totengeist,” explaining it as a representation of the living sign of the dead, someone who is preserved alive after death. Von Soden ([soden1979konflikte: 11, fn. 28]; [soden1978erste: 50-94]; [vonsoden1973mensch: 350-352]; [soden1989igigu: 344–348]; [vonsoden1991urmensch]) rejects the interpretation of eṭemmum as “Totengeist,” and instead reads the name of the primeval man in Atramḫasīs as Edimmu/Widimmu (based on SipOB2). This interpretation is followed by [cagnisangue: 79-80], who translates line 215 as “Dalla carne del dio (šīrum) sia fatto Edimmu”. [schramm1994review: 151], following this interpretation, suggests that the word (w)eṭemmum has a foreign etymology, and posits it as a possible origin for the name “Adam” in the Old Testament. Cagni, however, does not perceive a negative connotation in eṭemmum in this context ([RN1299: 21-22]). He emphasizes that the death of the god has a positive connotation. Contrary to the common scholarly view that eṭemmum always denotes a spirit or ghost with negative implications, Cagni suggests that in this context, eṭemmum has a vital meaning, linked to a living god whose blood and flesh are crucial for human creation. [RN1299: 22] notes that biblical passages on human creation (Gen. 1 and 2) omit any mention of death or death-related aspects. Further considerations on the reading and interpretation of e-ṭe-em-mu can be found in [RN1179: 68-69 with note 32]. [RN1780: 334-35] offers another interpretation, viewing the logographic writing of eṭemmum, GIDIM (a sign comprising the fraction ⅓ plus IŠ×TAR), as an unusual form of ištar(u), meaning “goddess,” and posits that eṭemmum could be either one-third goddess or one-third of a goddess. The variant form with an initial /w/ in MS SipOB2 is attributed by [RN1196: 102 fn. 73] to a late Babylonian phenomenon of initial /w/ loss: in MS SipOB2, the /w/ in we-ṭi-im-mu was incorrectly restored in antiquity. [veenhof1990interpretatie] offers a different view, interpreting the variant as an etymological wordplay between Wê – ṭēmum and the “spirit of the dead” (w)eṭemmmu. He also notes a connection between GIDIM and geštug, supported by an Old Babylonian text (@url{/fragmentarium/IM.74368}{IM.74368} ll. 35-36). A similar view is presented by [RN844: 29], associating GIDIM with Akk. eṭemmu(m) and attributing the SipOB2 variant to an originally palatal initial sound of the word.

212

  • N: balṭa | ittašu | lišēdīšū-ma
  • T: “Let it make the living know its sign,
  • L: balṭa ← balṭu I “living, alive”; ittašu ← ittu I “pl. idātu(m) ~ peculiarity? Bab., NA”; lišēdīšū-ma ← edû II “to know (M/NA cf. wadûm)”
  • Note: The exact interpretation of the term bal-ṭa in this verse is debated. The original interpretation by [RN435] understood balṭa as a living human, as the sign (ittu) of the spirit (eṭemmum), implying that the living human being is the expression of the spirit. Saggs ([Saggsencounter: 166]) rejected this interpretation, arguing that eṭemmum cannot convey vitality or a vital spirit, as it is consistently associated with ghosts or images of dead people in the sources. He understands bal-ṭa not as “living man” but rather as “a living thing” more generally. Saggs argues that the verse likely means that the eṭemmum manifests itself in the form of a living thing, with the eṭemmum, the ghost, resembling a living human being. He translates the line as “May it [scil. the eṭemmum] make known its sign (in the form of) a living thing.” On the other hand, Abusch ([abusch1998]) considers bal-ṭa to refer to the living person, which he believes is a combination of ṭēmum (representing the blood) and eṭemmum (the flesh). He translates the line as “To the living creature, let it make known its sign.”

Since products of the ḫaluppu-tree play a central role in therapies for a woman who does not become pregnant ([boeck2009proverbs: 275–276]), it is possible that the line refer to it; perhaps as an epithet of the “womb” (“the tree of the dynasty,” i.e. the place of origin of a lineage?). [RN7444: 426]: “palûm wäre dann hier eine Stange, die mit einer anderen zu einer Geburtszange (forceps) verbunden wäre.”] [jacobsen1973nintur: 230] (supported with reservations by [RN744: 115 fn. 30] and [RN1962: 167 no. 55]) understands this passage as a reference to the rupturing of the membranes by midwives and suggested restoring a construct state hu#-lu#-up pa-le-e “the insertion of the palû,” deriving palû from Sumerian bala, ‘spindle’, and understanding it as “a pointed implement” ([jacobsen1973nintur: 230 note 63]). [wilcke1985familiengruendung: 297 fn. 123], and apud [stol1983zwangerschap: 115, addenda to p. 56] (“sie zog (iḫlup) das Herrinengewand (palû) über,” see also [RN744: 115 fn. 30]) reads [i]h!-lu-up pa-le-e and assumes that it refers to some garment (palû) that is put on (ḫalāpu). [RN744: 115 fn. 30] follows Wilcke in reading a verbal form ih-lu-up at the beginning, but admits that iḫ- is not certain. So [RN744: 115] translates: “she slipped into (?) the palû, opened the membranes.” Stol also points out that the word silītum normally means “afterbirth”.

[RN744: 116] relates this passage to other texts in which strings of stones are placed around the hips of a woman who does not give birth easily. He admits that the verb rakāsu would be more appropriate in this context than ezēḫu, but explains the choice of ezēḫu because of the poetic language of the text. The suffix ša in qablīša has been taken by some scholars to refer to Mami; [RN164: 237] interprets that it refers to the mother (“She girded (the mother’s) middle as she pronounced a blessing.”).

  • N: anākū-mi | abni || īpušā | qātāya
  • T: “I am the one who created, my hands have made it!

  • Note: See [moran1971atrahasis: 58–59 fn. 3]: “On lines 289 ff. we would follow the suggestion (private communication) of Thorkild Jacobsen that in line 290 the qadištum is the mother after childbirth – [RN435], without comment: “Let the midwife rejoice in the prostitute’s house” – and that the whole passage deals, first, with a nine day celebration after childbirth in honor of the mother-goddess, then (299 ff.) with the resumption of sexual relations. On this basis we would propose that in line 299 the date of the latter is given (ina UD x.KAM, “on the X day”) and that in line 300 we restore li-ih-ti-[pu, “let the woman and her husband purify each other (themselves?)”. The [RN435] reading has been rightly criticized by [RN7444: 425-426 fn. 2], but his own proposal, liḫtī[da], “let them speak with one another”, yields, in our opinion, a meaning much too unspecific for the context. The purification we propose could refer to rites freeing the woman of her taboo and the man of any pollution through contact with her. The use of the G stative of ḫiāpum in connection with love (@url{VAT.10101}{KAR 158} rev. ii 11) and sex appeal ([RN775: 122: 96, 120; 124: 125]) is certainly relevant, but a more general meaning, “fair, handsome”, seems to have developed; cf. namrum, “shining” > “perfect, in excellent condition”. However, attractive as Jacobsen’s suggestion on qadištu in line 290 may be – and note the late variant ḫarištu, woman in confinement ([RN435: 62: 15]) – , also to be noted are the Middle Assyrian evidence ([weidner1954hof: 268: 11]) associating the qadištum (qadiltum)-function with the midwife, and the Old Babylonian evidence for a qadištum serving as a nurse (see most recently, [soden1957hebamme: 121]).” According to [lambert1992prostitution: 143], the line “suggests that the qadištu’s house served as a small maternity hospital. The Late Assyrian version evidently did not acknowledge such an institution and substituted another word [ina bīt ḫa-riš-ti, “in the mother-to-be’s house”] according to which women had their babies at home.” See also [RN744: 173]: “A few scholars are of the opinion that qadištu here refers to the “mother after childbirth” who, for this reason, is “sacred” (the verb qadāšu) and, instead of the well-known title of a religious woman, they translate “tabooed (woman)” ([jacobsen1973nintur: 292 fn. 73]; [moran1971atrahasis: 58 fn. 3]). It is only this line from Atra-ḫasīs that is amenable to such an interpretation, but it should be noted that the lines from our literary text deal with the general context of taboo. The closing lines stress strict observance of divine rules. We will suggest below that the house of the qadištu may, perhaps, have been a nursery.”

  • N: ummi (|) šerri || uharrû | ramānša
  • T: “And the mother of the baby is separated(?),
  • L: ummi ← ummu I “f. mother”; šerri ← šerru I “Nuzi pl. also f. (young) child baby”; uharrû ← arû VI “to cut off Bab.”; ramānša ← ramānu I “O/MA pl. f. self ramānšu himself, itself, ramānī, Ass. raminī…”
  • Note: The interpretation of this line follows [RN435: 63, 155], who propose the meaning of “to severe” for u₂-har-ru-u₂. [matous1967neuern: 14], on the other side, suggests to derive it from ḫarûm ([RN2720: 329a] harû(um) V “eingreifen”; [RN2721: Ḫ 118b]), not yet attested in D stem. [soden1978erste: 82] takes it as a D-stem of erû(m) “entblößen” with a specific sense of “ein Kind entbinden” (“Wo immer eine Gebärende gebiert, eine Mutter von Kindem selbst entbindet”; see [RN2720: 1433b] urrûm III; [RN2721: E 325a sub 2] “to conceive”), an interpretation rejected by [wilcke1985familiengruendung: 297 note 124] on the grounds that “hier von der Geburtshilfe die Rede ist.” Moreover, as noted by [RN164: 279], parsing the verb as derived from erû(m) seems incompatible with the writing u₂-ha-[ar-ru-u₂] of the SB version (SB III 60). [muses2: 202 on I 292] derives it from ḫerû D, “to hollow oneself” (“And the mother of the baby is delivered”); an interpretation abandoned in [RN164: 238 and 279] in favor of the one offered in [RN744: 116 fn. 35], viz. the verb (w)urrû(m), “to cut off” (“the mother separates herself from her child as if it were the branch of a tree (ḫarû). Compare, furthermore, the translations by [VeenhofAtr1970: 393]: “sichzelf verlossen”, and [RN235: 139], “sich abmühen”.

297-298

  • N: i t[aʾād? | s]assūram || i taʾād | kēšam
  • T: “[Always pra]ise the birth-goddess, praise Kesh.
  • L: i ← i I “let's”; t[aʾād? ← nâdu I “to praise, celebrate”; s]assūram ← šassūru I “pl. f.”; i ← i I “let's”; taʾād ← nâdu I “to praise, celebrate”; kēšam ← Keš I
  • Note: See the collation from photograph in [RN7444: 426 fn. 2] (confirmed by collation in [RN7456: 314]): “lies i ta-ad-di! ki!-tam (so E; A -ta-am!) “sie lege eine Matte hin!” di statt ki bieten alle drei Kopien von E und meine Lesung nach der Photographie; das etwas verdrückte ki-tam statt des bisher gelesenen -ša kann man auf der Photographie gut erkennen. Der in der Kopie gegebene senkrechte Keil nach ki-ta-am auf A ist gewiss nur von ra, das darüber steht, durchgezogen.” Compare also the collation in [RN2709: 537] (“E does not read ki!-tam!, and the DIŠ in A (despite “gewiss”, p. 425²) is not an overrun from the above -ra”) and [RN1447: 97–98] ([ki#/di#-ta#-am+DIŠ]), from which [RN7457: 100] (and [RN1763: 170]) concludes: “Auch L.s Zeichnung lässt meine Lesung ki-ta-am zu. Ein überzähliger senkrechter Keil am Ende bleibt unerklärlich; oder sollte er das Zahlzeichen ‘1’ (ištēn) sein?”. See, however, also [RN1447: 98]: “First sign can be KI or DI, but the following four wedges cannot form either of these signs, and the last three wedges are not UD, since in that sign the lower winkelhaken is bigger and precedes the smaller upper one.” See also [RN7457: 100] “Meine Lesung i ta-ad-di ki-tam ‘sie lege die Matte hin!’ wird auch durch L.s Kopie bestätigt.” A summary of different understandings of this line (e.g. nadû “to lay down” [[soden1978erste: 68 zu 298]] vs. nâdu “to praise” [[RN435: 64]] and kītu “reed mat” vs. kitû “linen cloth” vs. the city Keš) can be found in [RN744: 117–118 fn. 39], who defends the original interpretation of [RN435: 65] (“Without ceasing praise the birth-goddess, praise Kesh!”) because of parallelism. In view of the clear ke-e-ša₂ of the SB version (III 64), Lambert’s interpretation seems inescapable. One can perhaps interpret the verb ta-ad, uncorrected, as taʾād, a variant of the regular form of nâdu, “to praise” (tanād), which is attested in personal names of the type DN-luʾād (about which s. [RN617: 145 fn. 11], the derivation from âdu, “to take notice of” suggested there is difficult, since the preterite form of the verb is iʾīd, s. [RN27201: §107r*]). According to [RN744: 117 fn. 41] the sense of the praise is not the “resumption of sexual relations” (cf. [moran1971atrahasis: 58 fn. 3]) but the “mythical foundation of marriage”.

  • T: “In [their house], when the bed is laid,
  • L: ina ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; b[ītīšunu? ← bītu I “m.”; in]a ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; nadê ← nadû III “to throw (down)”; eršim ← eršu IV “f. bed”
  • Note: The reconstruction here follows [wilcke1985familiengruendung: 296], who translates: “In [ihren Häusern], indem sie Betten aufstellen”. On the basis of @url{/corpus/L/1/4/SB/II}{SB Gilgameš II} 111, [finkelstein1967ana: 133] restores: i-na bi-[it e-mi li-in]-na-di-e e-er-ši “In the [nuptial cham]ber let the bed be prepared.” [moran1971atrahasis: 58] assumes that the lacuna contains a date specifying the duration of the taboo on sexual relations following a birth, and translates: “on the X day” (i-na UD.x.KAM). This interpretation is rejected by ([RN744: 18 fn. 41]), who maintains that this passage pertains to marriage rites. See also [landsberger1968jungfraeulichkeit: 84], who compares the passage 299–304 with Gilgameš (@url{/corpus/L/1/4/OB/II#159}{OB 159–161}), in particular the occurrence of Išḫara in Gilgameš (@url{/corpus/L/1/4/OB/II#196-197}{OB 196–197}) and in Atraḫasīs OB I 304.
